Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : BM2342 : Biomolecular Characterisation Techniques { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: Conformation of Biological Macromolecules (6 contact hours)
Structure of proteins: Primary, Secondary, Tertiary, Quarternary Forces that determine protein structure Structure of Polysaccharides, Conformational analysis of proteins, Conformational analysis of nucleic acids.
Module 2: Optical Techniques (10 Contact hours)
Light Microscopy, Absorption Spectroscopy: Basics, Electronic states, Analysis of Biopolymers, effect of conformation on absorption Optical Activity Fluorescence Spectroscopy Infrared and Raman Spectroscopy
Module 3: Hydrodynamic Techniques (10 contact hours)
Ultracentrifugation, sedimentation, analysis of sedimentation measurements, viscometry, Molecular Sieve Chromatography, Ion exchange chromatography, Affinity chromatography, Hydrophobic interaction chromatography, Electrophoresis
Module 4: Scattering and Diffraction Techniques (10 contact hours)
X-ray scattering, X-ray diffraction, Crystal properties, X-ray crystallography, Structure determination of molecule, Electron Microscopy, Neutron Scattering

Course Objective

1 .

To understand and learn about principles governing major bio-characterization techniques used in the biotechnology and biomedical engineering.

Course Outcome

1 .

1. Students will be able to learn about various techniques used in biomolecular characterization
2. Students will be able to relate biomolecule characteristics to characterization techniques.
3. Students will be design a characterization methodology for a real world example biomolecule of choice.

7712.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : BM0001 : Fundamentals of Mechanobiology { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: Introduction to Biomechanics: Force vectors, Coplanar, collinear and concurrent forces, Moment and torque, Statics: Analysis of systems in equilibrium, and Applications of statistics to Biomechanics.
Module 2: Mechanics and Dynamics: Introduction to dynamics, Linear kinematics and kinetics, Angular kinematics and kinetics, Work-energy methods, Stress and strain, Computational biomechanics, Multiaxial Deformations and stress analysis, Stress transformation, Principle stresses, Failure theories, Torsion and Bending.
Module 3: Mechanobiology and Tissue Mechanics: Skeletal tissues (bone, articular cartilage, tendons and ligaments) remodeling, Gait analysis, Cellular cytoskeleton, Intracellular signalling, Cell migration, Durotaxis, Mechanotaxis, Chemotaxis and Mechanics of biomembranes.
Module 4: Molecular Mechanics and Dynamics, Continuum mechanics, Microstructural models, Constitutive laws, Electromechanical and physicochemical properties of tissues, Viscoelasticity, Models of Viscoelasticity, Fracture and Fatigue, and Experimental measurements of mechanical behaviour Cells and tissues.

Course Objective

1 .

To provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the basic biomechanical principles and their application in biological systems.
2 .

To equip students with knowledge and skills in mechanics and dynamics as they relate to biological materials and systems at various scales.
3 .

To explore the interplay between mechanical forces and biological responses, focusing on tissue mechanics and cellular behavior.
4 .

To advance students understanding of biomechanics at the molecular and continuum levels, integrating advanced material properties and experimental techniques.

Course Outcome

1 .

At the end of the course,
1. Students will be able to analyze and solve static and dynamic problems in biomechanics
2. Students will demonstrate proficiency in evaluating linear and angular motion
3. Students will be adept at describing how mechanical forces influence biological processes at the cellular and tissue level
4. Students will critically evaluate and apply advanced biomechanical theories, models, and experimental techniques to assess the mechanical behavior of cells and tissues

Essential Reading

1 .

NihatOzkaya and Margareta Nordin, Fundamentals of biomechanics: Equilibrium, Motion and deformation, 2nd Edi. Springer , 1999

2 .

Y.C Fung, Biomechanics – Mechanical Properties of Living Tissues, Springer , 1993

Supplementary Reading

1 .

Roger Bartlett, Introduction to Sports Biomechanics: Analysing Human Movement Patterns, Taylor and Francis , 2007

2 .

Christopher R. Jacobs, Hayden Huang, Ronald Y. Kwon, Introduction to Cell Mechanics and Mechanobiology, Garland Science , 2012

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CE6137 : Bio Geotechnics { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Natural origins of soils, Biological processes in soils, The geologic origin of a soil, its depositional mode and environment, thixotropic processes.
Use of biological process for changes in physical properties (density, gradation, porosity, saturation), conduction properties (hydraulic, electrical, thermal), mechanical properties (stiffness, dilation, compressibility, swell/shrink, cohesion, cementation, friction angle, erodibility, and soil-water characteristic curve), and chemical composition (buffering, reactivity, cation exchange capacity) of soils.
Development of a biomediated soil improvement technique bioaugmentation (where the required microbes are injected into the soil) and biostimulation (where natural microbes are stimulated) Biogeochemical and geotechnical models, management of treatment of by-products
Durability and longevity/reversibility of the process, and education of engineers and researchers.

Course Objective

1 .

Able to apply engineering knowledge
2 .

Problem analysis skill will be enhanced
3 .

Environment Impact and sustainable solution
4 .

Design/development of solutions for complex engineering problems

Course Outcome

1 .

1. Learn the geologic origin of soil, its biological processes and thixotropic processes.
2. Knowledge on the biological processes for changes in physical properties, conduction properties, mechanical properties and chemical composition of soil.
3. Development of biomediated soil improvement technique, bioaugmentation, biostimulation geotechnical models.

Charles Jensen, Bio- and Chemo- Mechanical Processes in Geotechnical Engineering, Institution of Civil Engineers , UK, 2014

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : PH1004 : Electromagnetic and Quantum Physics { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Coordinator :

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: (5 hours)
Vector Analysis: Gradient, divergence, curl, vector rules, line, surface and volume integration, The fundamental theorem on gradient, Gauss divergence theorem, and Stoke's theorem. Spherical and cylindrical coordinates, Dirac delta Function.
Module 2: (8 hours)
Electrostatics: Gauss law in electrostatics, divergence and curl of static electric field, conductors. Boundary conditions on electric field. Polarization, electric field of a polarized object, Gauss’s law in the presence of dielectrics. Susceptibility, permittivity, and dielectric constant.
Module 3: ( 5 hours)
Magnetostatics: Biot-Savart's law and Ampere's law, divergence and curl of static magnetic field. Boundary conditions on magnetic fields.
Module 4: ( 9 hours)
Electromagnetic waves: Electromagnetic induction, Faraday’s law, Maxwell's equations in vacuum. Electromagnetic waves in vacuum.
Module 5: ( 9 hours)
Quantum Mechanics: Particle nature of wave, Particle diffraction, Wave nature of particle, de Broglie waves, group waves, phase velocity & group velocity, Schrödinger Equation, Particle in a box.

Course Objective

1 .

The application of vector analysis for electromagnetic theory.
2 .

The basics of electrostatics and electric field of a polarized object.
3 .

The fundamentals of magnetostatics.
4 .

The concepts of electrodynamics, Maxwell's equations and the origin and behavior of electromagnetic waves.
5 .

The origin of quantum mechanics and its application

Course Outcome

1 .

At the end of the course, students will be able to:
CO1: Apply vector analysis techniques to solve problems in electromagnetic theory.
CO2: Gain a fundamental understanding of electrostatics.
CO3: Get a basic understanding and applications of magnetostatics.
CO4: Apply Maxwell's equations to study electromagnetic fields. Acquire knowledge about electromagnetic waves, including their nature, propagation, and applications.
CO5: Basics of quantum mechanics and its application

Subject {L-T-P / C} : EC6511 : Optical Communication and Networks { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: Introduction to Optical Networking: Principles and challenges of optical networking, Enabling technologies and building blocks
Module 2: Optical Network Architectures: Local, Access, and Metro Networks, Single-hop and Multi-hop Networks, Optical Access and Metro Networks
Module 3: Wavelength-Routed Optical Networks: Wide-area optical networks, Routing and Wavelength Assignment (RWA), Elements of virtual topology design

Explain the principles, architecture, and challenges of optical networks, including single-hop, multi-hop, and wavelength-routed networks.

Examine key building blocks of optical networking, such as Wavelength Division Multiplexing (WDM), routing, wavelength assignment, and virtual topology design.

Assess survivability techniques in WDM networks and evaluate performance metrics for network resilience and fault tolerance.

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : MM2102 : Phase Transformation { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module-I: Thermodynamics and Kinetics of solid state Phase transformation. ( 4 Hours)
Atomic models of Diffusion (1 Hour)
Module-II: Allotropy of Iron and Fe-C Phase diagram, Functions of alloying elements, Importance of Austenite Grain size Formation of Austenite, (5 Hours)
Module-III: TTT and CCT Diagrams, Homogeneous and Heterogeneous nucleations, Strain energy effects Overall Transformation Kinetics, Empirical equations, and Transformation kinetics for Interface-controlled and Diffusion-controlled growth. ( 5 Hours)
Module-IV: Pearlitic, Bainitic, and Martensitic Transformations (Mechanisms, Kinetics and Morphologies). Pearlitic transformation, Factors influencing pearlitic transformation, Mechanism of transformation, Nucleation and growth, Orientation relationship Bainitic transformation: Mechanism of transformation, Nucleation and growth, Orientation relationships, Surface relief, Classical and non-classical morphology, Effect of alloying elements Martensitic transformation: Characteristics of transformation, Thermodynamics and kinetics, Nucleation and growth, Morphology, Crystallography, Stabilization. (11 Hours)
Module-V: Strengthening mechanisms. ( 2 Hours)
Module-VI: Recovery, Recrystallization, Grain Growth, Annihilation of point imperfections, nucleation mechanism, and driving force for growth. ( 5 Hours)
Module-VII: Massive and Spinodal Decomposition ( 2 Hours)
Module- VIII: Mechanism and Kinetics of precipitation of age-hardenable alloys. ( 3 Hours)

Course Objective

1 .

To follow the thermodynamics and kinetics of phase transformations.
2 .

To understand the principle of austenitizations and the implication of different parameters on kinetics.
3 .

Understand various mechanisms of pearlitic, Baintitic, and martensitic Transformations in the Fe-C system.
4 .

To understand age-hardening and recrystallization processes.

Course Outcome

1 .

1. The course integrates the thermodynamics and mechanisms of different phase transformations to follow their importance in the structure-property relationship.
2. The course outlines the thermodynamic background of phase transformations.
3. Characteristic and morphological features are well demonstrated in the course outcome.
4. Different types of transformations especially in steels are cited to highlight the importance of phase and properties.
5. Mechanism and kinetics of precipitation hardening are well enumerated to understand its importance in designing materials to perform in the targetted areas of application.
6. Recrystallization annealing has been covered to cite its importance during the working of steels.

Essential Reading

D. A. Porter and K E Easterling, Phase Transformations in Metals and Alloys, CRC

2 .

V. Raghavan, Solid State Phase Transformations, PHI

Supplementary Reading

2 .
